extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and students of political theory, constitutional design, and history (particularly American and English readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative claims about what constitutes a right constitution and the qualities of free government; includes practical rules for evaluating political treatises and observations about institutions (titles, magistracies, mixed government).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty defined by impartial laws and tribunals
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberty of the people consists in two things, in the laws and the tribunals: when these prevail in a city, without favour, respect, or partiality, that city and its citizens are free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a state's freedom by whether laws and courts operate impartially, without favour or partiality; equality before the law is the core metric of civic liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clemency conditional on public safety
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtue of clemency is... commended in princes whenever pardon and mercy cannot cause an injury to the public, and give insolence to the daring to rise against the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure executive mercy by whether it risks public welfare or encourages lawlessness; pardon is a virtue only when it does not imperil the common good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetuity of a commonwealth requires prudence and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode of making a commonwealth perpetual, or of any long duration, is by prudence, which disposes and rules with manly energy, as well as with wise discernment. This can alone be performed in a state by means of justice, which distributes to every one his deserts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prospects for durable government by the prudence of rulers and the fairness of legal institutions distributing rewards and punishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation and broad selection of magistrates to guard against ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Two magistrates were therefore created; and that they might be sure to guard against ambition, they must be chosen in rotation every six months, two at a time, from each of the four quarters of the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional designs (short terms, rotation, geographic/quarterly selection) are recommended as safeguards against concentration of power and ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistrates/captains as protectors of plebeian liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: The captains of the people... were to be the protectors of the plebeians, and defenders of their liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate magistracies by whether they genuinely act as institutional protectors of common citizens' rights rather than agents of elite domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government (king, nobility, commons) as best form
rubrics_metrics.description: Ponnet... is clearly for a mixed government, in three equiponderant branches... where all together, that is a king, the nobilitie, and commons, a mixte state... had their distinct names... and which men by long continuance have judged to be the best sort of all: for where that mixte state was exercised, there did the commonwealthe longest continue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging constitutions, consider models that distribute power across monarchy, aristocracy, and popular representation; longevity is a supporting criterion for mixed regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual rule for reading political works
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one indispensable rule to be observed in the perusal of all of them; and that is, to consider the period in which they were written, the circumstances of the times, and the personal character as well as the political situation of the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate political arguments with attention to historical context, the author's aims and environment—avoid taking pamphlet arguments at face value without this calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles, orders, and honors require popular/constitutional sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: If these gentlemen had been of opinion that titles and ribbons were necessary in society, they should have taken measures for calling conventions of the people... and, lastly, there should have been in convention a general election of noblemen for each of the thirteen states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess legitimacy of creating hereditary titles or orders by whether they were instituted with public consent or constitutional process rather than by private or military self-authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice in distribution of fame and honors
rubrics_metrics.description: As great injustice may be done by giving too much honour to one, and too little to another, as by committing trespasses upon property, or slanders upon reputations, the public good requires justice in the distribution of fame as well as fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider equality and fairness in civic honors as part of public justice; evaluate institutions by their handling of reputation and reward as well as property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of monarchy characterized by governing through nobility and military control
rubrics_metrics.description: That the perfection of monarchy consists in governing by a nobility, weighty enough to keep the people under, yet not tall enough, in any particular person, to measure with the prince; and by a moderate army... sufficient to strangle all seditions in the cradle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising monarchical systems, note the structural reliance on a subordinate nobility and controlled military—this is a descriptive criterion of how monarchy seeks to maintain order (presented here as a theoretical model rather than normative endorsement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Government is vested in the person whose will gives being to the law (Hobbesian critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: It was contended, that to say that laws do or can govern, is to amuse ourselves... That the government is not in the law, but in the person whose will gives a being to that law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an interpretive lens: distinguish systems where law constrains rulers from those where law is an instrument of a sovereign will; evaluate institutional rule-of-law accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private officer-societies (e.g., orders) can exclude merit from civil life
rubrics_metrics.description: They have already excluded many excellent men from places in civil life, to which their merit in other respects entitled them; they have excited disputes which are very pernicious; they are founded on no principle of morals, true policy, or our own constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the civic impact of exclusive societies/privileged orders by whether they block competent individuals from civil roles, foster factional disputes, or lack moral/political justification.
